newsitem.title: CHINA: Sister asks Gore to appeal to China for dissident.
newsitem.headline: Sister asks Gore to appeal to China for dissident.

text.p: The sister of China's most prominent dissident has appealed to U.S. Vice President Al Gore to ask Beijing to free him from a 14-year jail term when he meets China's leaders in Beijing this week.

The health of veteran dissident Wei Jingsheng was deteriorating in a Chinese jail and his requests for medical care had been ignored by prison authorities, a U.S.-based human rights group quoted his family as saying after a recent visit.
In a letter to Gore, Wei's sister called on the U.S. Vice President to use the opportunity of his meetings this week with Chinese leaders to appeal for the release of her brother.

"I ask you to appeal to the Chinese government for my brother's prompt release and, until prior to his release, for his parole for medical treatment," wrote Wei Shanshan in a letter dated March 4 and a copy of which was made available by the New York-based Human Rights in China.
"My brother has already lost 18 of his 46 years in prison," she wrote. "I appeal to you to concern yourself about his fate to the greatest extent possible."
Wei was sentenced in December 1995 to 14 years in prison on charges of plotting to overthrow the government and is serving his term in a jail near the northern port city of Tianjin.
The veteran dissident was arrested in April 1994, just six months after he was released on parole after serving 14-1/2 years of a 15-year term for counter-revolutionary crimes -- or subversion.
Wei is regarded as the father of China's modern democracy movement and has been a nominee several times in recent years for the Nobel Peace Prize.
"Both houses of Congress passed resolutions that said the release of my brother should be one of the U.S. government's principal objectives," wrote Wei Shanshan, who lives in Germany.
Family members who visited him last week said Wei appeared to be suffering from neck pains and had difficulty holding up his head. However, prison officials said he did not need a medical check.

He was suffering from arthritis, high blood pressure and stomach problems but was receiving no treatment and had not undergone a medical check-up since February, 1996, the human rights group quoted Wei's brother and sister as saying after visiting him on March 21.
Wei was no longer sharing a cell with six criminals, but the men now lived in a neighbouring cell and watched him in four-hour, round-the-clock shifts, his family said.
He was allowed to read some domestically published history books but was not permitted books on philosophy or social affairs and was not allowed to write letters, his family said.
The date of the monthly family visit had been altered to ensure Wei's family would not be in Beijing during Gore's four-day visit this week, family members said.
Beijing is eager to ensure nothing mars the visit by Gore, the most senior U.S. official to travel to China in eight years.
Human rights abuses in China have long been a sore spot in Sino-U.S. relations, particularly since China called in the army to crush a student-led democracy movement in Beijing in 1989.
In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
Hong Kong newspapers have reported that Chinese authorities had offered recently to release dissident and former student leader Wang Dan on condition he leaves China.
Wang, a leader of the 1989 demonstrations, had agreed to China's condition and was expected to be released soon, the newspapers said. His family said they were unaware of such a deal.
